title: Generate usable ideas
summary: Generate relevant ideas from four dependable sources, then make each idea specific enough to develop without inventing false experience.

sections.title: Start inside the task contract
content: Return to the E6.1 task contract: ‘I will explain to secondary-school readers how one school-learned skill or idea applies in another area of life, using one specific actual or realistic example.’ Every idea in your pool must fit that boundary.
Idea generation is not yet paragraph ordering. First produce several possible examples quickly. E6.3 will compare them and choose the strongest sequence.

sections.title: Search four dependable sources
content: Use four sources when your mind feels blank. Experience is something you have done or seen directly. Observation is something you have noticed another person or group doing. School learning is a method, principle or habit learned through a subject. A plausible scenario is an honest, realistic situation in which you could apply the learning.
The prompt permits ‘have used’ or ‘could use’, so a plausible future scenario is valid when you signal it honestly. Do not present an invented event as a true memory.

sections.title: Turn a broad idea into usable evidence
content: Broad idea: ‘Mathematics teaches problem-solving, which is useful in life.’ This is relevant but too general to support a paragraph.

Usable idea: ‘I learned to break a multi-step mathematics problem into smaller parts. I could use the same method to organise a school charity sale by separating publicity, supplies, prices and staffing, then checking each part before the event.’
The second version identifies the learning, a different situation, a concrete action and a likely result. Those details give the writer material to explain rather than repeat a claim.

sections.title: Use the I-S-A-R frame
content: Build each candidate with four notes: Idea, Situation, Action and Result or learning. Idea names the school-learned skill. Situation places it outside the original lesson. Action shows what the writer did or could do. Result or learning explains why the transfer matters.

Example: Idea—breaking a task into parts. Situation—planning a charity sale. Action—divide the work into publicity, supplies, prices and staffing. Result—fewer missed tasks and a clearer way to solve problems under pressure.
A result does not need to be dramatic. A clearer decision, avoided mistake or changed understanding can be enough.

sections.title: Build a three-idea pool
content: Set a four-minute limit and produce three candidates from different sources. For each one, write a one-line I-S-A-R frame. Keep the same decoded task contract visible while you work.
Do not reject an idea merely because it is ordinary. A precise everyday example is more useful than an impressive claim with no action or evidence. Leave comparison and ordering until E6.3.

sections.title: Reject unusable ideas
content: Off-task ideas do not answer the task contract. Vague ideas name a benefit without a situation or action. Thin ideas contain a situation but no detail that can be explained. Fabricated experience presents an invented past event as fact.

Repair an off-task idea by reconnecting it to the chosen school learning. Repair a vague or thin idea by adding the situation and action. Repair a fabricated experience by changing it into an honestly signalled possibility, such as ‘I could use this when…’.

sections.title: Generate before you choose
content: Use the E6.1 task contract to test six idea-generation decisions. Complete the group before viewing feedback, then keep the strongest corrected I-S-A-R frames for E6.3.
